title: In the 1100s, a Native American city in Illinois rivalled London in size

cover.alt: Monks Mound at Cahokia: a huge, flat-topped, grass-covered earthen mound with a long staircase up its side, rising beyond a green meadow under a blue sky.

body: Cahokia, directly across the Mississippi River from present-day St. Louis, was a Native American city that existed from about 1050 to 1350. At its peak around 1100 it spread over some 6 square miles with about 120 earthworks, and its population, usually put at 15,000 to 20,000, was comparable to London’s at the time. Its centrepiece, **Monks Mound**, is the largest human-made earthen mound north of Mexico, raised higher and wider over several centuries. By about 1350 the city had emptied, probably through a mix of social and environmental causes.

slides.question: How tall is Monks Mound?
slides.explanation: About 30 m high, 290 m long and 255 m wide. It holds roughly 622,000 cubic metres of earth.

slides.label: area covered by the base of Monks Mound, about 13.8 acres
slides.text: It grew in as many as ten construction episodes over several centuries.

slides.heading: How many people lived in Cahokia at its peak?
If the highest guess is right
slides.text: At 40,000 people, Cahokia would have been larger than any later city in the United States until the 1780s, when Philadelphia grew past that size.

slides.alt: A tall wooden post standing alone in a mown green field, with a wide ring of thinner posts behind it: the reconstructed Woodhenge at Cahokia.
slides.caption: The reconstructed ‘Woodhenge’, a ring of timber posts about 850 m west of Monks Mound. The site holds public sunrise watches at the equinoxes and solstices.

slides.question: About how many earthworks did Cahokia have at its peak?
slides.explanation: About 120. Some 80 man-made mounds survive in today’s 2,200-acre park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1982.
